key_points: Unsaturated hydrocarbons undergo addition reactions due to the presence of double or triple bonds
marking_schemes.model_answer: Unsaturated hydrocarbons undergo addition reactions, where other molecules add across the double or triple bond without any atom being removed.
common_errors: Some candidates chose substitution reaction (characteristic of saturated hydrocarbons)
A few chose oxidation reaction
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Teach the difference between unsaturated and saturated hydrocarbons and highlight their reactivity and types of reactions. Facilitate revision using structural diagrams.

marking_schemes.scheme_text: (d) / D / The outer most shell is completely filled.
key_points: Neon has maximum ionization potential in period 2 because its outermost shell is completely filled (stable electronic configuration)
marking_schemes.model_answer: Neon has the maximum ionization potential in the second period because its outermost shell is completely filled, giving it a stable electronic configuration that strongly resists the removal of an electron.
accepted_alternatives: The outermost shell is completely filled
common_errors: A few candidates chose option (a) — 'It has unstable electronic configuration' — the opposite of the correct reason
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Emphasize that ionization potential increases across a period due to greater nuclear charge. Highlight that Neon, at the extreme end of period 2, has the highest ionization potential. Stress reasons behind maximum ionization potential in noble gases.

key_points: Bronze is an alloy of copper, zinc, and tin
Note: The marking scheme also accepts Brass (Cu + Zn) — candidates who chose Brass were also credited
marking_schemes.model_answer: Copper, Zinc, and Tin alloyed together form Bronze. (Note: the marking scheme also accepted Brass as an alternative answer.)
common_errors: Some candidates confused brass and bronze
A few chose duralumin instead
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Clearly explain the differences in alloy compositions and their uses, emphasizing the primary metal in each alloy. Provide revision of the compositions of alloys.

marking_schemes.scheme_text: (c) / C / Aluminium hydroxide / Al(OH)3 / Aluminium / Al
key_points: Aluminium hydroxide is amphoteric — it reacts with both acids and alkalis to form salt and water
marking_schemes.model_answer: The metal hydroxide that reacts with both acids and alkalis to form salt and water is Aluminium hydroxide, Al(OH)3. This amphoteric behaviour distinguishes it from basic-only hydroxides like Ca(OH)2 and Mg(OH)2.
common_errors: A few selected calcium hydroxide or magnesium hydroxide, which are not amphoteric
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain the concepts of acidic, basic, amphoteric, and neutral oxides with equations. Highlight the differences between amphoteric and other metallic hydroxides.

key_points: The reaction of an alcohol with a carboxylic acid in the presence of concentrated H2SO4 is called esterification
marking_schemes.model_answer: The reaction of an alcohol with a carboxylic acid in the presence of concentrated H2SO4 to produce an ester and water is termed esterification.
common_errors: Many chose dehydrohalogenation
Some chose hydrogenation or halogenation
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain organic compound reactions and their conditions, ensuring adequate revision. Stress the difference between dehydrohalogenation (removal of halogen and water) and esterification.

key_points: Conversion of ethanol to ethene by concentrated H2SO4 involves dehydration — removal of water
marking_schemes.model_answer: The conversion of ethanol to ethene by concentrated sulphuric acid involves dehydration — the removal of a water molecule from the ethanol molecule.
common_errors: Many incorrectly chose dehydrogenation
Candidates were confused between dehydrogenation and dehydrohalogenation
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Stress the difference between dehydration (removal of water only) and dehydrogenation (removal of hydrogen). Explain each with examples and equations.

key_points: In S + 2H2SO4 → 3SO2 + 2H2O, sulphur is oxidized (S→SO2), so H2SO4 is the oxidizing agent
marking_schemes.model_answer: The oxidizing agent in the equation S + 2H2SO4 → 3SO2 + 2H2O is sulphuric acid (H2SO4). Sulphur is oxidized from 0 to +4, so H2SO4 acts as the oxidizing agent.
common_errors: Many candidates incorrectly chose sulphur dioxide, confusing product with oxidizing agent
Candidates struggled with identifying oxidizing agents from equations
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Clarify oxidation-reduction concepts and the roles of oxidizing and reducing agents using equations. Provide practice identifying oxidizing agents with H2SO4 equations.

marking_schemes.scheme_text: (d) / D / Br / bromine / Br2 / br2 / br
key_points: Electron affinity is maximum in bromine (Br) among the given options
Noble gases (Ar) have zero electron affinity; Li and Mg have low electron affinity
marking_schemes.model_answer: Electron affinity is maximum in Bromine (Br) among the given options. Noble gases like Ar have zero electron affinity, while metals like Mg and Li have very low values. Bromine, as a halogen, has a strong tendency to gain electrons.
common_errors: Majority chose Ar or Li instead of Br
Candidates were unaware that noble gases have zero electron affinity
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Use multiple examples and emphasize exceptional cases. Clarify that inert gases have zero electron affinity and no tendency to attract electrons.

marking_schemes.scheme_text: (b) / B / NaAlO2 / sodium aluminate / sodium meta aluminate
key_points: The Hall-Heroult electrolytic mixture contains Al2O3 (alumina), Na3AlF6 (cryolite), and CaF2 (fluorspar)
NaAlO2 (sodium aluminate) is NOT a constituent of this mixture
marking_schemes.model_answer: The compound that is NOT a constituent of the electrolytic mixture used in the Hall-Heroult process is NaAlO2 (sodium aluminate). The mixture consists of Al2O3 dissolved in molten Na3AlF6 (cryolite), with CaF2 (fluorspar) added to lower the melting point.
common_errors: Many chose Al2O3 instead
Some chose Na3AlF6 due to unfamiliarity with the formula
Some overlooked the word 'not' in the question
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Emphasize the steps involved in metal extraction from ores. Explain aluminium extraction in detail. Provide practice writing the formula and components of the Hall-Heroult electrolytic mixture. Instruct students to read questions carefully and pay attention to bold or italicized words.

marking_schemes.scheme_text: (c) / C / Reducing property / Reducing agent / Reducing
key_points: Ammonia reduces copper oxide (CuO) to copper (reddish-brown residue), demonstrating its reducing property
marking_schemes.model_answer: Ammonia passing over heated copper oxide demonstrates its reducing property. Ammonia reduces CuO to copper (the reddish-brown residue), while itself being oxidized to nitrogen and water.
common_errors: Many confused reducing property with basic property or oxidizing property
Several incorrectly identified ammonia as an oxidizing agent
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Clearly explain the fundamental differences between the basic nature and reducing property of ammonia. Emphasize teaching through practical experiments to help students retain facts.

key_points: Rotten egg smell is due to hydrogen sulphide (H2S) gas
marking_schemes.model_answer: The rotten egg smell is due to the liberation of hydrogen sulphide (H2S) gas.
common_errors: A few chose SO2 or HCl
Some incorrectly associated the rotten egg smell with HCl gas
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Emphasize identification of gases by smell and color. Provide regular objective tests to avoid mistakes. Encourage experimental learning to help students recognize and recall lab observations.

key_points: Ammonia is lighter than air (molar mass = 17 g/mol vs air ≈ 29 g/mol)
It is collected by downward displacement of air (upward delivery into the jar)
marking_schemes.model_answer: Ammonia gas is collected by downward displacement of air because it is lighter than air (molar mass 17 g/mol compared to air at approximately 29 g/mol).
common_errors: Some wrote 'heavier than air'
Others cited its solubility in water as the reason — solubility explains why it cannot be collected over water, not why downward displacement is used
Few confused ammonia collection with HCl collection
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Create a comparative chart of HCl and NH3 to clarify their collection methods and properties. Explain when to use upward or downward displacement of air or water during gas collection.

marking_schemes.scheme_text: (b) / B / 1 & 3 / or 32 gm of oxygen gas and 6.022 x 10^23 molecules of ammonia
key_points: 32 g of O2 = 1 mole → occupies 22.4 L at STP ✓
2 moles of H2 would occupy 2 × 22.4 = 44.8 L at STP ✗
6.022 × 10^23 molecules of NH3 = 1 mole → occupies 22.4 L at STP ✓
Therefore options 1 and 3 each occupy 22.4 L; option 2 does not
marking_schemes.model_answer: Options 1 and 3 each occupy 22.4 L at STP. 32 g of O2 = 1 mole (molar mass = 32); 6.022 × 10²³ molecules of NH3 = 1 mole. 2 moles of H2 would occupy 44.8 L, not 22.4 L.
accepted_alternatives: 32 g of oxygen and 6.022×10^23 molecules of ammonia
common_errors: Many selected option C (2 & 3) or D (all three) without working out calculations
Several did not calculate and guessed
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Discourage guesswork and encourage solving problems. Provide relevant examples and repetitive practice to differentiate between moles, molecules, and volumes at STP.

marking_schemes.scheme_text: (c) / C / Two lone pairs of electrons / 2
key_points: Oxygen in water has 6 valence electrons: 2 are used in 2 shared pairs (O–H bonds), leaving 2 lone pairs
marking_schemes.model_answer: In the water molecule, the oxygen atom has two lone pairs of electrons. Of its six valence electrons, two are shared in covalent bonds with hydrogen atoms and four remain as two lone pairs.
common_errors: Many chose one lone pair — incorrect
A few confused the lone pairs in ammonia (1 lone pair) with water (2 lone pairs)
Some incorrectly assumed hydrogen has lone pairs
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Provide relevant examples and repetitive practice to differentiate between lone pairs and shared pairs of electrons. Draw structures of compounds to explain the types of electron pairs.

key_points: An ore is a mineral from which a metal can be extracted economically and conveniently
marking_schemes.model_answer: A mineral from which a metal can be extracted economically and conveniently is known as an ore.
common_errors: A few confused the term with alloy or matrix
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Emphasize learning the names of important ores and clarify terms related to metallurgy. Ensure students understand the processes and correct definitions with key words.

marking_schemes.scheme_text: The metal gets deposited / The metal ion gets discharged at the cathode / nickel ions or cations move to the cathode / Ni²⁺ gets discharged / reduction takes place at the cathode / cathode acts as reducing electrode.
key_points: The iron cup is placed at the cathode because reduction takes place there
Ni²⁺ ions in the electrolyte migrate to the cathode and are discharged (reduced to Ni metal), depositing on the iron cup
marking_schemes.model_answer: The iron cup is placed at the cathode because reduction occurs at the cathode. Nickel ions (Ni²⁺) from the electrolyte migrate to the cathode, are discharged (gain electrons), and are deposited as nickel metal on the iron cup.
common_errors: Most failed to state the actual reason — only said 'the article to be plated is at the cathode' without explaining why
Used 'discharged' vs 'deposited' incorrectly
Some confused reducing electrode with oxidizing electrode
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain the concept of electroplating clearly, detailing where the article to be plated should be placed and how ions are deposited. Elucidate the roles of anode and cathode with equations.

key_points: The electrolyte must contain Ni²⁺ (nickel ions) so that nickel can be deposited at the cathode
marking_schemes.model_answer: The ion that must be present in the electrolyte is Ni²⁺ (nickel ion). These ions migrate to the cathode and are reduced to nickel metal, coating the iron cup.
common_errors: Some provided incorrect valency for nickel
Others incorrectly wrote iron (Fe) as the ion present
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Clearly explain element valencies and ions present in electrolytes. Emphasize the concept of ion migration to specific electrodes.

marking_schemes.scheme_text: Small / low current for a long period of time / DC should be used / AC should not be used / high current for short period of time should not be used / article should be thoroughly cleaned / article should be dipped completely in the electrolyte
key_points: Use low/small current for a long period of time
Use DC (direct current), not AC
Article must be thoroughly cleaned before electroplating
Article must be completely immersed in the electrolyte
marking_schemes.model_answer: To ensure a smooth, firm, and even deposit, a low current should be passed for a long period of time using direct current (DC). The iron cup must also be thoroughly cleaned and completely submerged in the electrolyte.
common_errors: A few incorrectly mentioned using large or high current
Some wrote 'slow current for a long time' — incomplete phrasing
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Lay emphasis on the use of DC for smooth and uniform electroplating and the use of low current for a long period. Explain all conditions necessary for a smooth and firm metal deposit.

key_points: At the cathode, nickel ions are reduced: Ni²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Ni
marking_schemes.model_answer: The reaction at the cathode is: Ni²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Ni. Nickel ions gain two electrons and are deposited as nickel metal.
common_errors: Many were confused by the valency of Ni
A few wrote the equation in reverse (Ni → Ni²⁺) — which is the anode reaction
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Discuss the differences between simple electrolysis, electroplating, and electrorefining. Provide practice in writing reactions at cathode and anode for clarity.

marking_schemes.scheme_text: The anode decreases in mass / size / becomes thinner / diminishes / reduces / dissolves / used up
key_points: The nickel anode dissolves into the electrolyte, decreasing in mass/size as electroplating proceeds
marking_schemes.model_answer: At the anode, nickel metal dissolves into the electrolyte as Ni²⁺ ions, causing the anode to decrease in mass and size (it diminishes).
common_errors: A few incorrectly wrote 'no change' or 'no reaction' due to lack of awareness of the process
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain the products and changes at the anode and cathode. Detailing observations with both inert and active electrodes is essential.

marking_schemes.scheme_text: Column A: (a) Water → 3. Covalent compound; (b) Alkali metal → 1. Lithium; (c) Halogen → 2. Iodine; (d) Calcium oxide → 5. Ionic compound; (e) Weak acid → 4. Acetic acid
key_points: (a) Water → 3. Covalent compound
(b) Alkali metal → 1. Lithium
(c) Halogen → 2. Iodine
(d) Calcium oxide → 5. Ionic compound
(e) Weak acid → 4. Acetic acid
marking_schemes.model_answer: Water is a covalent compound (3); an alkali metal is Lithium (1); a halogen is Iodine (2); calcium oxide is an ionic compound (5); a weak acid is acetic acid (4).
common_errors: Some confused water as ionic and calcium oxide as covalent
A few mixed up halogen (iodine) and alkali metal (lithium)
Some incorrectly identified sulphuric acid as a weak acid
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Teach the basic concept of covalent and ionic compounds. Explain halogens and alkali metals with their names and symbols. Give examples of weak and strong acids.

key_points: FeCl3 (ferric chloride) is prepared by direct combination of iron and chlorine
FeCl2 (ferrous chloride) cannot be prepared by direct combination under normal conditions
marking_schemes.model_answer: The salt that can be prepared by direct combination is FeCl3 (ferric chloride / Iron(III) chloride). Iron reacts directly with excess chlorine to form ferric chloride.
common_errors: Many incorrectly answered FeCl2 instead of FeCl3
Candidates confused ferrous and ferric chloride in relation to direct combination
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Ensure enough practice with the six methods of salt preparation, including examples and correct equations. Emphasize identifying which iron chloride is formed by direct combination.

marking_schemes.scheme_text: Fe2O3 / ferric oxide / Iron(III) oxide / Fe / Iron
key_points: Fe2O3 (iron oxide) can be reduced by common reducing agents like CO, H2, or coke
Al2O3 cannot be reduced by common reducing agents — it requires electrolysis
marking_schemes.model_answer: The metallic oxide that can be reduced by using common reducing agents is Fe2O3 (ferric oxide). Al2O3 is too stable and cannot be reduced by common reducing agents — it requires electrolytic reduction.
common_errors: Many incorrectly chose Al2O3 instead of Fe2O3
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain the differences in stability between metallic oxides and the reducing agents required. Al2O3 requires electrolysis whereas Fe2O3 can be reduced by coke/CO.

marking_schemes.scheme_text: Copper nitrate / Cu(NO3)2 / Copper(II) nitrate / Copper / Cu / cupric nitrate
key_points: Copper nitrate on thermal decomposition forms CuO (black residue), NO2, and O2
Zinc nitrate on decomposition forms ZnO (white/yellow residue), not black
marking_schemes.model_answer: The metal nitrate that on thermal decomposition forms a black residue is copper nitrate, Cu(NO3)2. The black residue is copper oxide (CuO): 2Cu(NO3)2 → 2CuO + 4NO2 + O2.
common_errors: Most confused copper nitrate with zinc nitrate, mistakenly believing zinc nitrate gives a black residue
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Conduct quizzes and provide practice on thermal decomposition of metal nitrates. Teach the products and colour of residues for each nitrate.

key_points: When copper electrodes are used in electrolysis of CuSO4 solution, the anode dissolves and cathode gains mass, keeping the concentration — and hence colour — of the electrolyte constant
marking_schemes.model_answer: When copper electrodes are used, the colour of the copper sulphate electrolyte does not fade because the copper deposited at the cathode is replenished by the copper dissolving at the anode, maintaining the concentration of Cu²⁺ ions.
common_errors: Most candidates correctly identified copper; a few were confused about the role of electrode material in maintaining electrolyte concentration
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain the products and changes at the anode and cathode with both inert (platinum) and active (copper) electrodes. Clarify why the colour fades with inert electrodes but not with active ones.

key_points: Calcination is the process of heating a concentrated ore in a limited supply or absence of air
Roasting involves heating in excess air
marking_schemes.model_answer: The process of heating a concentrated ore in a limited supply or absence of air is calcination. This is distinct from roasting, which involves heating in excess air.
common_errors: Many candidates confused roasting and calcination
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Conduct quizzes and provide practice on processes like roasting and calcination in metallurgy, clearly defining each.

key_points: The group obtained by removing one hydrogen atom from the parent alkane is called an alkyl group (general formula CnH2n+1)
marking_schemes.model_answer: The group obtained by removing one hydrogen atom from the parent alkane is called an alkyl group (e.g., –CH3, –C2H5).
common_errors: Some confused the term and wrote 'alkyne'
Some gave an example of the group rather than the term
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Familiarize students with terms and their derivatives: alkyl, alkane, alkene, and alkyne. Clearly explain these concepts with various examples.

key_points: The two metal plates or wires through which current enters and leaves the electrolytic cell are called electrodes (cathode and anode together)
marking_schemes.model_answer: The two metal plates or wires through which current enters and leaves the electrolytic cell are called electrodes (the cathode and the anode collectively).
common_errors: Most candidates wrote 'cathode and anode' — this is acceptable but some simply wrote just 'electrodes' without specifying both
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Ensure students understand all terms involved in electrolysis and stress on their functions.

key_points: The amount of substance containing the same number of units as atoms in 12 g of carbon-12 is defined as one mole (Avogadro's number = 6.022 × 10²³ units)
marking_schemes.model_answer: The amount of substance which contains the same number of units as the number of atoms in carbon-12 (i.e., 6.022 × 10²³ units) is called a mole (one mole).
common_errors: Majority failed to write 'mole' — most wrote 'relative molecular mass' instead
Candidates were confused by the statement referring to carbon-12
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Insist on learning definitions and familiarize students with all terms in the syllabus, especially RMM, RAM, mole, Avogadro's law, Gay-Lussac's law, gram atom, vapour density, etc.

key_points: The tendency of an atom to pull a shared pair of electrons towards itself in a compound is called electronegativity
marking_schemes.model_answer: The tendency of an atom to pull a shared pair of electrons towards itself when bonded in a compound is called electronegativity.
common_errors: Some confused it with electron affinity — electron affinity is the energy released when an isolated atom gains an electron
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Teach property trends with clear definitions. Ensure a thorough understanding of the distinction between electronegativity and electron affinity.

key_points: The formula representing the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound is the empirical formula
marking_schemes.model_answer: The formula which represents the simplest ratio between the atoms of elements present in a compound is called the empirical formula.
common_errors: Many incorrectly answered 'molecular formula' — the molecular formula shows the actual number of atoms, not the simplest ratio
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Emphasize the concept that the simplest ratio of atoms in a compound is its empirical formula. Distinguish it clearly from the molecular formula.

key_points: 5-carbon chain (pentane backbone)
Chlorine atoms at positions 2 and 3
Two Cl atoms = prefix 'dichloro'
IUPAC name: 2,3-dichloropentane
marking_schemes.model_answer: The IUPAC name of the compound is 2,3-dichloropentane. It has a 5-carbon chain with chlorine substituents at positions 2 and 3.
common_errors: Most wrote '2-chloro, 3-chloropentane' instead of '2,3-dichloropentane'
Some wrote 'pentene' instead of 'pentane'
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Acquaint students with naming compounds according to the IUPAC system. Familiarize students with the basic rules, including selecting the longest chain and using prefixes like 'di' and 'tri'.

key_points: 3-carbon chain
Carboxylic acid functional group (–COOH) at C1
IUPAC name: propanoic acid
marking_schemes.model_answer: The IUPAC name of the compound is propanoic acid (propan-1-oic acid). It is a 3-carbon carboxylic acid with the –COOH group at carbon 1.
common_errors: Most confused propanoic acid with propanol or propanal
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Stress the importance of IUPAC nomenclature. Ensure correct placement of functional groups. Emphasize that carboxylic acids end in '-oic acid'.

marking_schemes.scheme_text: 3-methylpentane structural formula: 5-carbon chain with CH3 branch at C3. Accepted forms: full structural, semi-structural (H3C-CH2-CH(CH3)-CH2-CH3), or condensed.
key_points: 5-carbon main chain (pentane)
Methyl group (–CH3) at carbon 3
All carbon valencies satisfied
Correct number of hydrogen atoms shown
marking_schemes.model_answer: 3-methylpentane has a 5-carbon main chain with a methyl group branching off the third carbon. Its structural formula shows: CH3–CH2–CH(CH3)–CH2–CH3, with all C–H and C–C bonds explicitly drawn.
accepted_alternatives: full structural diagram with correct H placement
common_errors: A few misplaced the methyl group
Some forgot to include the correct number of hydrogen atoms
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Emphasize regular practice in drawing structures. Ensure correct placing of functional groups. Train students to draw structural formulas ensuring all carbon atoms satisfy their tetravalency.

marking_schemes.scheme_text: Propyne structural formula: H-C-C≡C-H (with CH3 group on one carbon and triple bond shown). Or CH3-C≡CH.
key_points: 3-carbon chain
Triple bond (C≡C) between C2 and C3
Carbon at C1 has 3 H atoms (CH3 group)
Carbon at C3 has 1 H atom
marking_schemes.model_answer: Propyne (C3H4) has a triple bond between the second and third carbons. Its structural formula is: CH3–C≡CH, with the methyl group at one end and the triple bond shown explicitly.
accepted_alternatives: full structural diagram showing C≡C triple bond
common_errors: Several candidates failed to show carbon's tetravalency in the structure
Some drew a double bond instead of a triple bond
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Demonstrate carbon as tetravalent. Provide ample practice through quizzes and structure-writing exercises.

marking_schemes.scheme_text: Methanal structural formula: H-C(=O)-H or H2C=O
key_points: 1-carbon aldehyde
Carbon double bonded to oxygen (C=O)
Two hydrogen atoms bonded to carbon
Full structural formula: H–C(=O)–H
marking_schemes.model_answer: Methanal (HCHO) is the simplest aldehyde with one carbon atom double bonded to oxygen and two hydrogen atoms. Its structural formula is H–C(=O)–H (or H2C=O).
accepted_alternatives: full structural diagram showing C=O double bond
common_errors: Many candidates failed to depict the double bond for oxygen and drew a single bond instead
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Emphasize that oxygen is bivalent and the carbonyl group (C=O) must show a double bond. Stress correct placement and representation of functional groups.

marking_schemes.scheme_text: Concentrated Sulphuric acid acts as a dehydrating agent.
key_points: The word 'Concentrated' must be added before 'Sulphuric acid'
marking_schemes.model_answer: Concentrated sulphuric acid acts as a dehydrating agent.
accepted_alternatives: Concentrated H2SO4 acts as a dehydrating agent
common_errors: Many wrote only the word 'concentrated' without completing the full sentence
Some failed to rewrite the full corrected statement
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Teach all properties of sulphuric acid with examples. Guide students to read questions properly and answer in full sentences as instructed.

marking_schemes.scheme_text: Excess ammonia reacts with chlorine to give ammonium chloride and nitrogen.
key_points: The word 'Excess' (or 'Excess of') must be added before 'ammonia'
Excess ammonia + Cl2 → NH4Cl + N2; excess chlorine + NH3 → NCl3 + HCl
marking_schemes.model_answer: Excess ammonia reacts with chlorine to give ammonium chloride and nitrogen.
accepted_alternatives: Excess of ammonia reacts with chlorine to give ammonium chloride and nitrogen
common_errors: Many mistakenly added 'aqueous' instead of 'excess'
Candidates confused the two reactions: excess ammonia with Cl2 and excess Cl2 with ammonia
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Teach reactions with clear conditions. Emphasize 'excess ammonia with chlorine' and 'excess chlorine with ammonia' as separate reactions with different products and equations.

marking_schemes.scheme_text: Carbonate / Bicarbonate / hydrogen carbonate / CO3²⁻ / HCO3⁻
key_points: Gas produced turns lime water milky → CO2 → anion is carbonate (CO3²⁻) or bicarbonate/hydrogen carbonate (HCO3⁻)
No effect on acidified potassium dichromate → confirms it is not SO2 (sulphite/sulphate ruled out)
marking_schemes.model_answer: The anion present is carbonate (CO3²⁻) or hydrogen carbonate (HCO3⁻). The colourless, odourless gas that turns lime water milky is CO2, and carbonate/bicarbonate salts produce CO2 on heating. The absence of effect on acidified K2Cr2O7 rules out sulphite.
common_errors: Many failed to identify the correct anion
Some provided the correct valency but wrong formula
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Familiarize students with the practical test for CO2 starting with lime water test followed by the acidified dichromate solution test. Teach how to identify anions through confirmatory tests.

key_points: The Brown Ring test (conc. H2SO4 + freshly prepared FeSO4 solution → brown ring) is specific to nitrate ions (NO3⁻)
marking_schemes.model_answer: The anion present is nitrate (NO3⁻). The Brown Ring test — treating the solution with concentrated H2SO4 and freshly prepared ferrous sulphate solution — is a confirmatory test for the nitrate ion.
common_errors: Most failed to write the correct anion as nitrate
Some wrote the ion symbolically but with incorrect valencies
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Demonstrate the Brown Ring test using freshly prepared ferrous sulphate solution to detect the presence of nitrate. Teach anion and cation formation through practical work.

key_points: pH < 7 indicates an acidic solution, which reacts with magnesium to liberate hydrogen
Both R (pH 2) and Q (pH 5) are acidic and would liberate H2 gas with Mg
marking_schemes.model_answer: Solutions R (pH 2) and Q (pH 5) will react with magnesium to liberate hydrogen gas, as both are acidic (pH < 7). Solution P (pH 13) is alkaline and will not react with magnesium to give H2.
common_errors: Some incorrectly identified only one of the two acidic solutions
A few were confused about which solutions are acidic based on pH
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Acquaint students with the pH scale that represents the concentration of H3O⁺ in solution. Provide various metals for practice on equations and gas formation.

key_points: An alkaline solution (pH > 7) liberates ammonia gas from ammonium chloride on heating
P has pH 13 — strongly alkaline
marking_schemes.model_answer: Solution P (pH 13) will liberate ammonia gas when it reacts with ammonium chloride, as it is a strongly alkaline solution (pH > 7). The reaction: NH4Cl + NaOH → NaCl + NH3 + H2O.
common_errors: A few candidates incorrectly wrote R/2 — acidic solutions do not liberate ammonia from ammonium chloride
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Teach the gases formed from reactions with ammonia and other acidic gases. Explain their nature, state, and properties using a table.

key_points: A weak acid (pH 5) is partially dissociated — it contains both molecules AND ions
A strong acid (pH 2, R) is almost fully dissociated — contains mainly ions
A strong alkali (pH 13, P) is fully dissociated — contains only ions
Therefore Q (weak acid, pH 5) contains both molecules and ions
marking_schemes.model_answer: Solution Q (pH 5) contains both molecules and ions. At pH 5, the solution is a weak acid that is only partially dissociated — both undissociated acid molecules and ions coexist.
common_errors: Many answered R or P incorrectly
Most were confused about the particles present based on whether a solution is strong or weak acid/base
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain about the particles present in compounds — whether molecules, ions, or both — with respect to their bonding and degree of dissociation. Connect pH to strength of acid/base.

marking_schemes.scheme_text: (a) Contact process / oxidation / catalytic oxidation; (b) Vanadium Pentoxide / V2O5 / Platinum / Pt; (c) Sulphuric acid / H2SO4 / SO3 / sulphur trioxide
key_points: (a) The process is the Contact Process (catalytic oxidation of SO2 to SO3)
(b) The catalyst is Vanadium Pentoxide (V2O5) or Platinum (Pt)
(c) The final product is Sulphuric acid (H2SO4) — or SO3 as intermediate
marking_schemes.model_answer: The industrial process is the Contact Process (catalytic oxidation of SO2). The catalyst (b) is Vanadium Pentoxide (V2O5). The final product (c) is sulphuric acid (H2SO4), produced via SO3 as an intermediate.
accepted_alternatives: (c) H2SO4, Sulphuric acid, SO3, sulphur trioxide
common_errors: Some confused the Contact Process with the Ostwald Process or Bayer's Process
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Emphasize every step of the Contact Process for preparing sulphuric acid in detail. Provide practice of all industrial processes according to the syllabus. Create a table to differentiate processes by name, reactants, products, catalyst, and special conditions.

marking_schemes.scheme_text: Molar Volume – Volume occupied by 1 gm molecular weight of a gas / or one mole of a gas at S.T.P.
key_points: Molar volume is the volume occupied by one mole (1 g molecular mass) of a gas at STP
Value = 22.4 L at STP
marking_schemes.model_answer: Molar volume is the volume occupied by one gram-molecular mass (one mole) of a gas at standard temperature and pressure (STP). Its value is 22.4 litres.
accepted_alternatives: Volume occupied by 1 mole of a gas at STP
Volume occupied by 1 g molecular weight of a gas at STP
common_errors: Many did not include STP/NTP in their answer
Some confused molar volume with relative molecular mass
Others did not specify that it applies to gases only
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Emphasize that the molar volume of a gas is the volume occupied by one gram-molecular mass or one mole of a gas at STP. Stress that molar volume applies only to gases.

marking_schemes.scheme_text: Normal Salt: The salts formed by complete / total replacement of the hydrogen of an acid molecule by a basic / base radical / metallic / ammonium ion. / Salt formed by complete neutralization of an acid by a base.
key_points: Normal salt is formed by complete replacement of all replaceable hydrogen ions of an acid
The replacement is by a metallic ion, basic radical, or ammonium ion
Equivalent: complete neutralization of an acid by a base
marking_schemes.model_answer: A normal salt is formed by the complete replacement of all the replaceable hydrogen atoms of an acid molecule by a metallic or ammonium ion (i.e., by complete neutralization of an acid by a base), leaving no hydrogen capable of further replacement.
accepted_alternatives: Salt formed by complete neutralization of an acid by a base
complete replacement of all replaceable H atoms by metal/ammonium ion
common_errors: Many failed to use the key phrase 'complete replacement of replaceable hydrogen ion'
Most only stated 'acid reacts with base to form salt and water' without specifying the completeness of replacement
Many did not specify 'an acid molecule by a basic radical/ammonium ion/metallic'
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Guide students by demonstrating in practical classes how to prepare normal salt through complete replacement of the hydronium ion by a metal ion or a base. Train students with correct definitions containing all keywords.

marking_schemes.scheme_text: Electron dot structure of methane (CH4): C has 4 shared pairs with 4 H atoms. Different symbols for C electrons (dots) and H electrons (crosses).
key_points: Carbon (4 valence electrons) forms 4 shared pairs with 4 hydrogen atoms
Each H contributes 1 electron; carbon contributes 1 electron to each bond
Electrons from C and H shown with different symbols (dots and crosses)
No lone pairs on carbon
marking_schemes.model_answer: The electron dot structure of methane shows carbon (represented by dots) sharing one electron each with four hydrogen atoms (represented by crosses), forming four covalent bonds. No lone pairs remain on carbon.
accepted_alternatives: Any correct dot-and-cross diagram with distinct symbols for C and H electrons
common_errors: Many depicted covalent bonds between dots or between dot and cross (drawing a line between them)
Some used the same symbol for both elements
Some drew orbital structures instead of electron dot diagrams
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Provide ample practice of drawing electron-dot structures. Emphasize drawing different elements with distinct notations as dots and crosses, ensuring bonds are not drawn as lines between them.

marking_schemes.scheme_text: Electron dot structure of nitrogen molecule (N2): triple bond between two N atoms, each with one lone pair. Notation: :N:::N: or :N≡N:
key_points: Each N atom has 5 valence electrons
3 electrons from each N are shared to form a triple bond
Each N retains 1 lone pair (2 electrons)
Correct notation: :N:::N: with lone pairs shown on each nitrogen
marking_schemes.model_answer: The electron dot structure of nitrogen (N2) shows two nitrogen atoms each with 5 valence electrons forming a triple bond (3 shared pairs) between them, with one lone pair remaining on each nitrogen atom.
common_errors: Some correctly drew the triple bond but forgot to include the lone pair on each nitrogen
Many drew orbital structures instead
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Provide ample practice through short quizzes, board work, and classroom activities to master drawing electron structures, including single, double, and triple bonds. Guide students to differentiate annotations on different elements.

key_points: Al2O3 is amphoteric — reacts with NaOH (base) to form sodium aluminate
Products: sodium aluminate (NaAlO2) and water
Balanced: Al2O3 + 2NaOH → 2NaAlO2 + H2O
marking_schemes.model_answer: Al2O3 reacts with NaOH to form sodium aluminate and water: Al2O3 + 2NaOH → 2NaAlO2 + H2O.
common_errors: Many incorrectly wrote aluminium hydroxide and sodium oxide as products
Many were confused with the formula for sodium aluminate (NaAlO2)
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Ensure students understand amphoteric oxides and their properties. Advise students to write clear chemical reactions noting gases formed and necessary conditions.

marking_schemes.scheme_text: C2H5COONa + NaOH → C2H6 + Na2CO3 [condition: CaO, Δ]
key_points: Sodium propanoate + NaOH (with CaO, heated) → ethane + sodium carbonate
This is the laboratory preparation of alkanes (decarboxylation)
Balanced: C2H5COONa + NaOH → C2H6 + Na2CO3
marking_schemes.model_answer: Sodium propanoate reacts with NaOH in the presence of CaO on heating to form ethane and sodium carbonate: C2H5COONa + NaOH → C2H6 + Na2CO3.
common_errors: Most balanced the equations correctly; a few made errors or over-balanced them
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Provide ample practice for completing and balancing equations of alkanes, alkenes, and alkynes with emphasis on necessary conditions in organic chemistry.

key_points: Dehydrohalogenation with alcoholic KOH removes 2 HBr molecules from 1,2-dibromoethane
Product: acetylene (C2H2 / ethyne), KBr, and water
Balanced: C2H4Br2 + 2KOH (alcoholic) → C2H2 + 2KBr + 2H2O
marking_schemes.model_answer: 1,2-dibromoethane reacts with alcoholic KOH (double dehydrohalogenation) to form ethyne, potassium bromide, and water: C2H4Br2 + 2KOH(alc.) → C2H2 + 2KBr + 2H2O.
common_errors: Many wrote C2H6 instead of C2H2 as the product
Some failed to balance the equation
Some wrote hydrogen instead of water as a product
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Stress the difference between products formed with aqueous KOH (substitution) and alcoholic KOH (elimination). Explain organic compound preparation with balanced equations and conditions.

key_points: Ethanol (C2H5OH) has no double bond in its structure — it is a saturated compound with –OH functional group
marking_schemes.model_answer: Ethanol (C2H5OH) does not have a double bond in its structure. It is a saturated compound, unlike ethene (C=C double bond) and methanal (C=O double bond).
common_errors: Some chose methanal or ethanoic acid instead of ethanol
Some misidentified ethene because of its double bond, without reading the question carefully
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Familiarize students with organic compound properties to match descriptions with correct options. Guide students to read questions carefully.

marking_schemes.scheme_text: Ethanoic acid / acetic acid / glacial acetic acid / CH3COOH
key_points: Ethanoic acid (CH3COOH) in pure form solidifies to a colourless ice-like solid (glacial acetic acid) below 16.6°C
marking_schemes.model_answer: Ethanoic acid (acetic acid, CH3COOH) in its pure form turns into an ice-like solid (glacial acetic acid) on cooling below 16.6°C.
common_errors: Some chose other options from the list incorrectly
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain properties of key organic compounds like ethanoic acid (glacial acetic acid upon cooling) and discuss its uses.

key_points: Ethene (C2H4) is used for artificial ripening of fruits — it is the plant hormone responsible for ripening
marking_schemes.model_answer: Ethene (C2H4 / ethylene) is the compound used for artificial ripening of fruits. It acts as a plant hormone that accelerates the ripening process.
common_errors: A few mistakenly chose ethanol
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Discuss the impact of chemicals in daily life, explaining terms with relevant examples. Elucidate the diverse uses of organic compounds.

key_points: Duralumin is an alloy based on aluminium (Al) as the primary metal, with copper, magnesium, and manganese
marking_schemes.model_answer: The main metal used in making Duralumin is Aluminium (Al). Duralumin is a lightweight, high-strength aluminium alloy.
common_errors: A few listed additional components without emphasizing aluminium as the primary metal
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Conduct regular quizzes to reinforce memory of alloy components and properties. Teach alloys ensuring students understand the composition and the main (base) metal in each.

key_points: Stainless steel is an alloy based on iron (Fe) as the primary metal, with chromium, nickel, and carbon
marking_schemes.model_answer: The main metal used in making Stainless steel is Iron (Fe). Stainless steel is an iron alloy containing chromium, nickel, and carbon.
common_errors: Some listed additional alloy components without highlighting iron as the primary metal
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Clearly explain metals and other components used in stainless steel, emphasizing that carbon is the only non-metal used.

marking_schemes.scheme_text: Sulphuric acid forms a ppt / insoluble substance or Barium sulphate when treated with BaCl2 but HNO3 does not form any ppt / forms soluble substance / no such observations / no visible change.
key_points: Add BaCl2 solution to both acids
H2SO4 forms a white precipitate of BaSO4 (insoluble)
HNO3 forms no precipitate — barium nitrate is soluble
marking_schemes.model_answer: When barium chloride solution is added, sulphuric acid produces a white precipitate of barium sulphate (BaSO4), which is insoluble. Nitric acid produces no precipitate as barium nitrate is soluble.
accepted_alternatives: H2SO4 forms white ppt of BaSO4; HNO3 forms no ppt
common_errors: Many were unable to differentiate using BaCl2
Several failed to note the absence of a precipitate with nitric acid
Some incorrectly noted a brown precipitate with nitric acid
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Demonstrate the BaCl2 test in the lab for sulphate ions. Clarify distinctions between acids including dilution and concentration differences along with equations and observations.

marking_schemes.scheme_text: Unsaturated hydrocarbons have a double or triple bond whereas a saturated hydrocarbon has only single bonds. = bond or ≡ bond / - bond. Or correct structure / examples / carbon skeleton.
key_points: Unsaturated hydrocarbons contain double (C=C) or triple (C≡C) bonds
Saturated hydrocarbons contain only single (C–C) bonds
marking_schemes.model_answer: Unsaturated hydrocarbons contain at least one double bond (C=C) or triple bond (C≡C), while saturated hydrocarbons contain only single bonds (C–C) between carbon atoms.
accepted_alternatives: double or triple bond vs single bond
correct structural examples demonstrating bond types
common_errors: A few confused the concepts and provided incorrect answers or gave examples without stating the bond type difference
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Ensure students grasp the distinctions between saturated and unsaturated organic compounds by emphasizing bond types and electron availability.

key_points: Mass = moles × molar mass = 5 × 100 = 500 g
marking_schemes.model_answer: Mass of 5 moles of CaCO3 = 5 × 100 = 500 g.
common_errors: Some wrote the answer directly as '500 grams' without showing the calculation step '5 × 100'
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Guide students to do step-by-step numerical problem-solving and provide ample practice. Explain the equivalence between moles, molar mass, and molar volume.

key_points: From the equation CaCO3 + 2HCl → CaCl2 + H2O + CO2, 1 mole CaCO3 reacts with 2 moles HCl
5 moles CaCO3 requires 5 × 2 = 10 moles HCl
marking_schemes.model_answer: From the stoichiometry of the equation, 1 mole of CaCO3 reacts with 2 moles of HCl. Therefore 5 moles of CaCO3 will react with 5 × 2 = 10 moles of HCl.
common_errors: A few made errors in calculation or omitted this part entirely
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Guide students on balancing equations and selecting the correct components to calculate mole numbers in compound-based questions.

key_points: 1 mole CO2 occupies 22.4 L at STP
5 moles of CaCO3 produce 5 moles of CO2
Volume = 5 × 22.4 = 112 L at STP
marking_schemes.model_answer: 5 moles of CaCO3 produce 5 moles of CO2. At STP, 1 mole of gas occupies 22.4 L. Therefore volume of CO2 = 5 × 22.4 = 112 L (or 112,000 mL).
common_errors: Many just wrote 22.4 L without multiplying by 5 (only considering 1 mole)
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain how to use the standard volume of 22.4 litres in calculations based on the given equations. Encourage thorough solutions with correct units.

key_points: Complete combustion of methane (CH4) produces CO2 and H2O
CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O
marking_schemes.model_answer: When methane undergoes complete combustion, carbon dioxide (CO2) and water are produced. The gas evolved is carbon dioxide.
common_errors: A few identified it as carbonate (CO3²⁻) — a solid ion, not a gas
Some may have written carbon monoxide
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Stress on the products formed on complete combustion of organic compounds as carbon dioxide and water.

key_points: CuCO3 heated → CuO (black) + CO2 gas
CO2 turns lime water milky
marking_schemes.model_answer: When copper carbonate is heated, carbon dioxide (CO2) is evolved along with a black residue of copper oxide. The gas evolved is carbon dioxide.
common_errors: A few wrote carbon monoxide instead of carbon dioxide
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Provide hands-on experience of the decomposition of carbonates through experiments. Emphasize that CO2 turns lime water milky but does not affect acidified potassium dichromate solution.

marking_schemes.scheme_text: Cl2 / Chlorine / Cl / greenish yellow gas
key_points: MnO2 + 4HCl (conc.) → MnCl2 + 2H2O + Cl2 ↑
Chlorine gas (Cl2) is evolved — pungent, greenish yellow
marking_schemes.model_answer: When MnO2 reacts with concentrated HCl, chlorine gas (Cl2) is evolved. It is a pungent, greenish yellow gas that turns moist starch iodide paper blue-black.
common_errors: While most wrote 'Chlorine' correctly, many lost marks by writing the formula as Cl (monatomic) instead of Cl2 (diatomic)
Some wrote 'chloride ion'
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Emphasize that chlorine gas is diatomic (Cl2). Explain the reaction with observations and equations. Explain the reaction of MnO2 with conc. HCl clearly.

key_points: Electrolytic dissociation: pre-existing ions in an ionic lattice separate when the compound is melted or dissolved
PbBr2 is an ionic compound — its ions are already formed in the lattice; melting causes dissociation
marking_schemes.model_answer: Reaction Y (PbBr2 ⇋ Pb²⁺ + 2Br⁻ in molten state) exhibits electrolytic dissociation. PbBr2 is an ionic compound whose pre-existing ions separate upon melting.
common_errors: A few confused electrolytic dissociation with ionization and chose X
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Emphasize that metals typically have 1, 2, or 3 valence electrons while non-metals have 4, 5, 6, or 7. Stress that metal-non-metal bonds are ionic, leading to electrolytic dissociation.

key_points: Ionization: covalent molecules (like HCl) form ions when dissolved in a solvent — no pre-existing ions
HCl is a covalent molecule that ionizes in aqueous solution
marking_schemes.model_answer: Reaction X (HCl ⇋ H⁺ + Cl⁻ in solution) exhibits ionization. HCl is a covalent molecule that does not contain pre-existing ions; it forms ions only when dissolved in water.
common_errors: Majority failed to recognize that X undergoes ionization and confused it with electrolytic dissociation
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Clarify the distinction between electrolytic dissociation (ionic compounds, pre-existing ions) and ionization (covalent molecules forming ions in solution). Explain where each occurs.

marking_schemes.scheme_text: Because their outermost shell is complete / they have stable electronic configuration / they do not lose or donate electrons / octet or duplet state.
key_points: Inert gases have completely filled outermost shells (octet/duplet)
This stable configuration means they have no tendency to gain, lose, or share electrons — hence no ion formation
marking_schemes.model_answer: Inert gases do not form ions because their outermost electron shell is completely filled (octet or duplet configuration), giving them a stable electronic configuration with no tendency to gain or lose electrons.
accepted_alternatives: do not lose or gain electrons
common_errors: A few simply wrote 'because they are inert' or 'cannot participate in chemical reactions' without giving the electronic configuration as the reason
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Emphasize that inert gases do not form ions or react due to their stable electronic configuration. Clearly explain the stability of noble gases compared to other elements.

marking_schemes.scheme_text: Because they have a weak force of attraction / Van der Waal's force of attraction between the molecules / particles.
key_points: Covalent compounds have weak Van der Waals forces between molecules (not between atoms within the molecule)
These weak intermolecular forces require little energy to overcome, hence low melting and boiling points
marking_schemes.model_answer: Covalent compounds have low melting and boiling points because they have weak Van der Waals forces of attraction between their molecules. Little energy is needed to overcome these weak intermolecular forces.
accepted_alternatives: weak Van der Waals forces between molecules
common_errors: Most failed to use the correct keyword 'Van der Waals forces'
Many wrote 'weak electrostatic forces' or 'less force/attraction' without specifying they are between molecules
Many did not specify 'between the molecules'
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain the concept and meaning of electrostatic force vs Van der Waals forces with their nature and where they exist. Emphasize differences between properties of electrovalent and covalent compounds.

marking_schemes.scheme_text: Beryllium, Carbon, Fluorine / Be, C, F / Be>, C>F (decreasing order of atomic size)
key_points: Atomic size decreases across a period (left to right)
In period 2: Be (group 2) > C (group 14) > F (group 17)
Decreasing order: Be > C > F
marking_schemes.model_answer: In decreasing order of atomic size: Beryllium > Carbon > Fluorine (Be > C > F). Atomic size decreases across a period from left to right due to increasing nuclear charge.
common_errors: Many wrote the sequence in reverse (increasing) order
Some confused the greater/lesser symbols
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Emphasize the periodic trend of properties across a period from left to right, relating to electronic configuration. Provide regular practice on arranging elements by periodic properties.

marking_schemes.scheme_text: Acetic acid, Sulphuric acid, Phosphoric acid (increasing order of number of replaceable H atoms per molecule)
key_points: Acetic acid (CH3COOH): 1 replaceable H atom (monobasic)
Sulphuric acid (H2SO4): 2 replaceable H atoms (dibasic)
Phosphoric acid (H3PO4): 3 replaceable H atoms (tribasic)
Increasing order: acetic acid < sulphuric acid < phosphoric acid
marking_schemes.model_answer: In increasing order of number of replaceable H atoms per molecule: acetic acid (1) < sulphuric acid (2) < phosphoric acid (3).
accepted_alternatives: Acetic acid < Sulphuric acid < Phosphoric acid
common_errors: Many failed to correctly arrange the acids in order
Some confused the basicity of each acid
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Focus on the basicity of an acid — the number of hydronium ions produced by one molecule in aqueous solution. Teach students to identify monobasic, dibasic, and tribasic acids.

marking_schemes.scheme_text: Potassium, Sodium, Lithium / K < Na < Li / K, Na, Li (increasing order of ionization potential)
key_points: Ionization potential increases up the group (smaller atoms have higher ionization potential)
Increasing order: K < Na < Li
Li has the smallest atomic size among these and the highest ionization potential
marking_schemes.model_answer: In increasing order of ionization potential: Potassium < Sodium < Lithium (K < Na < Li). Ionization potential increases up Group 1 as atomic size decreases.
common_errors: Many wrote it in reverse (decreasing) order without correct symbols
A few were confused with the property trend of ionization potential down the group
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Provide sequential practice questions with different criteria to reinforce understanding. Teach periodic table trends, focusing on properties across periods and down groups. Emphasize the importance of writing correct symbols < and >.

key_points: Hydrogen (H) is in period 1 and can be placed in group 1 (1 valence electron, like alkali metals) or group 17 (needs 1 electron to complete duplet, like halogens)
marking_schemes.model_answer: Hydrogen (H) is the element in period 1 that can be placed in both group 1 (as it has 1 valence electron like alkali metals) and group 17 (as it needs 1 more electron to complete its duplet shell, like halogens).
common_errors: A few incorrectly wrote lithium
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Familiarize students with all properties and exceptions. Teach students the periodic table trends, focusing on hydrogen's unique dual placement.

key_points: Electronic configuration 2, 8, 6 → 16 electrons total → atomic number 16 → Sulphur (S)
marking_schemes.model_answer: The element with electronic configuration 2, 8, 6 has 16 electrons, giving it atomic number 16, which corresponds to Sulphur (S).
common_errors: A few were confused by the atomic number and electronic configuration, resulting in incorrect identifications
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Encourage students to memorize elements up to atomic number 20 and provide ample practice with their electronic configurations.

key_points: In period 3, electronegativity increases from left to right
Chlorine (Cl, group 17) is the most electronegative element in period 3 (fluorine is the most electronegative overall but is in period 2)
marking_schemes.model_answer: The most electronegative element of period 3 is Chlorine (Cl). Electronegativity increases across a period, and chlorine (group 17) has the highest electronegativity in period 3.
common_errors: Many confused and incorrectly identified fluorine or bromine (not in period 3)
Some chose chlorine correctly but confused with the overall most electronegative element (fluorine)
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Emphasize the importance of understanding electronic configuration and placement in the periodic table. Provide ample practice on trends across periods and down groups.

key_points: Reddish-brown precipitate with ammonium hydroxide is a confirmatory test for Fe³⁺ (ferric ions)
Fe³⁺ + 3NH4OH → Fe(OH)3 (reddish-brown ppt) + 3NH4⁺
marking_schemes.model_answer: The cation present is Fe³⁺ (ferric / Iron(III)). The reddish-brown precipitate formed with ammonium hydroxide is iron(III) hydroxide, a confirmatory test for the ferric ion.
common_errors: Many misunderstood the question about cation and answered incorrectly
Some wrote Fe²⁺ (ferrous) instead of Fe³⁺ (ferric)
Many omitted the charge on the element, simply writing 'Iron' or 'Fe'
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Emphasize the formation of insoluble reddish-brown precipitate, specific to ferric ions, when treated with NaOH or NH4OH. Familiarize students with practical demonstrations.

key_points: White precipitate with silver nitrate solution indicates presence of Cl⁻ (chloride) or SO4²⁻ (sulphate)
AgCl is a white precipitate insoluble in water — confirms chloride
marking_schemes.model_answer: The anion present is Cl⁻ (chloride). The white precipitate formed with silver nitrate solution is silver chloride (AgCl), a confirmatory test for the chloride ion. (Sulphate is also accepted.)
common_errors: Many misunderstood and listed both cation and anion in both parts
Some only identified the cation in part (b) without identifying the anion
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Emphasize that silver nitrate is used to detect chloride ions by forming a white precipitate of silver chloride. Engage students in hands-on laboratory experience.

key_points: CCl4 is a symmetric tetrahedral molecule — the bond dipoles cancel out, making it a non-polar covalent molecule
marking_schemes.model_answer: Carbon tetrachloride (CCl4) is a non-polar covalent molecule. Despite having polar C–Cl bonds, the tetrahedral symmetry causes the bond dipoles to cancel, resulting in a non-polar molecule overall.
common_errors: A few confused it with polar and answered incorrectly
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Emphasize that when a bond forms between dissimilar atoms with a small electronegativity difference in a symmetric arrangement, it results in non-polar covalent compounds. Clearly differentiate between polar and non-polar covalent compounds.

key_points: During electrolysis of acidulated water, oxygen gas is liberated at the anode (oxidation)
Hydrogen is liberated at the cathode (reduction)
marking_schemes.model_answer: During electrolysis of acidulated water, oxygen (O2) is liberated at the anode. Water molecules are oxidized at the anode to give O2, while H⁺ ions are reduced at the cathode to give H2.
common_errors: A few were confused about the products at the anode and cathode and incorrectly answered hydrogen
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Provide ample examples and ensure practice of reactions at the cathode and anode under different conditions.

marking_schemes.scheme_text: O2 used = (3/4) × 240 = 180 cc. Excess O2 = 300 – 180 = 120 cc. N2 produced = (2/4) × 240 = 120 cc. Resultant mixture contains 120 cc of O2 and 120 cc of N2.
key_points: From 4NH3 + 3O2 → 2N2 + 6H2O, ratio NH3 : O2 : N2 = 4 : 3 : 2
O2 required for 240 cc NH3 = (3/4) × 240 = 180 cc (O2 is in excess: 300 cc available)
Excess O2 = 300 – 180 = 120 cc
N2 produced = (2/4) × 240 = 120 cc
Water condenses (liquid at room temperature) — not counted in gaseous mixture
Resultant gaseous mixture: 120 cc N2 + 120 cc O2
marking_schemes.model_answer: O2 consumed = (3/4) × 240 = 180 cc. Since 300 cc O2 was available, excess O2 = 300 – 180 = 120 cc. N2 produced = (2/4) × 240 = 120 cc. Water is liquid at room temperature. The resultant gaseous mixture contains 120 cc of O2 and 120 cc of N2.
common_errors: Some calculated O2 used and excess but failed to calculate N2 produced
Some noted N2 as 120 cc but ignored the excess O2
Some calculated only the oxygen consumed (180 cc) without continuing to find excess
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Emphasize that Gay-Lussac's Law applies only to gases, not liquids or solids (water condenses at room temperature). Ensure adequate practice of various numericals with regular stepwise working insisted upon.

key_points: A is 2,8,8,2 → atomic number 20 → Calcium (Ca), valency 2
B is 2,6 → atomic number 8 → Oxygen (O), valency 2
Formula using given letters: AB; chemical identity: CaO
marking_schemes.model_answer: Element A (configuration 2,8,8,2 — Calcium, valency 2) combines with element B (configuration 2,6 — Oxygen, valency 2) to form compound AB (CaO — calcium oxide).
common_errors: Some wrote the formula as 'A2B2' instead of 'AB'
Most candidates identified the elements but did not write the formula using the given letters as instructed
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Instruct students not to identify the given elements until asked. Facilitate practice of forming formulas using the given letters. Insist on writing the given letter to answer questions.

key_points: D is 2,4 → atomic number 6 → Carbon (C), valency 4
C is 2,8,7 → atomic number 17 → Chlorine (Cl), valency 1
Formula using given letters: DC4; chemical identity: CCl4
marking_schemes.model_answer: Element D (configuration 2,4 — Carbon, valency 4) combines with four atoms of element C (configuration 2,8,7 — Chlorine, valency 1) to form DC4 (CCl4 — carbon tetrachloride).
common_errors: Most correctly answered with the formula but many wrote 'CCl4' instead of 'DC4' as required by the question format
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Provide more practice with different examples to help students understand and correctly answer questions based on electronic configuration. Emphasize writing formulas based on the provided information.

key_points: Catenation is the property of an atom to form long chains with itself
Carbon (element D, configuration 2,4) exhibits catenation — it can form long chains and rings with other carbon atoms
marking_schemes.model_answer: Element D (Carbon) exhibits catenation. Carbon has the unique ability to form long chains, branched chains, and rings by bonding with other carbon atoms, a property called catenation.
common_errors: Some selected multiple options from the table and answered incorrectly
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain catenation and the elements that exhibit it, including reasons. Emphasize that carbon is the primary element known for catenation due to the strength and stability of C–C bonds.

key_points: Haematite (Fe2O3) is an iron ore that can be concentrated by magnetic separation because iron is magnetic
marking_schemes.model_answer: The ore that can be concentrated by magnetic separation is haematite (Fe2O3). Iron ores are magnetic and thus respond to magnetic separation.
common_errors: A few incorrectly chose zinc blende
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Emphasize learning the names of ores used in extracting important metals and the concentration method applicable to each ore.

key_points: Ethyne (C2H2): ratio of C:H = 2:2 = 1:1
Empirical formula = CH
marking_schemes.model_answer: The empirical formula of ethyne (C2H2) is CH, representing the simplest whole-number ratio of carbon to hydrogen atoms (1:1).
common_errors: Many incorrectly wrote the molecular formula C2H2 as the empirical formula instead of the simplified ratio CH
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Acquaint students with the empirical formula — the simplest formula showing the simplest whole number ratio of atoms. Emphasize the distinction between molecular and empirical formulae.

key_points: Copper reacts with concentrated HNO3 to produce copper nitrate, water, and nitrogen dioxide
Balanced equation: Cu + 4HNO3(conc.) → Cu(NO3)2 + 2H2O + 2NO2↑
marking_schemes.model_answer: Copper reacts with concentrated nitric acid to form copper nitrate, water, and nitrogen dioxide gas: Cu + 4HNO3(conc.) → Cu(NO3)2 + 2H2O + 2NO2.
common_errors: Many were unable to provide balanced equations
Some wrote the reaction for dilute HNO3 (which gives NO) instead of concentrated (which gives NO2)
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Demonstrate how concentrated nitric acid oxidizes copper. Explain the differences between dilute and concentrated reactions of copper with nitric acid, including products and observations.

key_points: Aluminium nitride reacts with warm water to produce aluminium hydroxide and ammonia gas
Balanced: AlN + 3H2O → Al(OH)3 + NH3
marking_schemes.model_answer: Aluminium nitride reacts with warm water to form aluminium hydroxide and ammonia: AlN + 3H2O → Al(OH)3 + NH3.
common_errors: Some incorrectly wrote aluminium oxide as the product
A few struggled with the correct formula for aluminium nitride (AlN)
Others had trouble identifying the correct products
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Teach the preparation of ammonia with metal nitrides as an alternative laboratory method. Provide frequent short tests and worksheets with equations.

key_points: ZnCl2 from Zn: zinc displaces hydrogen from HCl to form ZnCl2
Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl2 + H2↑ — this is a displacement reaction
marking_schemes.model_answer: ZnCl2 from Zn is prepared by displacement reaction (method 3). Zinc displaces hydrogen from dilute hydrochloric acid: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl2 + H2.
common_errors: Many incorrectly chose combination or neutralization reaction
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Emphasize that salts of active metals can be prepared by displacement reactions, where dilute acids react with active metals. Demonstrate these reactions to help students retain the facts.

key_points: KNO3 from KOH: potassium hydroxide (soluble base) reacts with dilute HNO3 by neutralization
KOH + HNO3 → KNO3 + H2O
marking_schemes.model_answer: KNO3 from KOH is prepared by neutralization (method 4). Potassium hydroxide (a soluble base) reacts with dilute nitric acid: KOH + HNO3 → KNO3 + H2O.
common_errors: A few confused it with direct combination or displacement reaction
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Familiarize students with the general solubility of salts and emphasize that titration is used for neutralization reactions with soluble bases.

key_points: CaCO3 from CaCl2: CaCO3 is insoluble — prepared by mixing two soluble salt solutions
CaCl2 + Na2CO3 → CaCO3↓ + 2NaCl — precipitation reaction
marking_schemes.model_answer: CaCO3 from CaCl2 is prepared by precipitation (method 1). Mixing calcium chloride solution with sodium carbonate solution produces an insoluble precipitate of calcium carbonate: CaCl2 + Na2CO3 → CaCO3↓ + 2NaCl.
common_errors: A few incorrectly answered direct combination or neutralization
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Illustrate preparing insoluble salts through precipitation methods, emphasizing the solubility of salts and reasons for each method. Teach students to prepare calcium carbonate through precipitation reactions.

key_points: Reactants: NaCl and concentrated H2SO4
Products: NaHSO4 and HCl
Condition: below 200°C (gentle warming)
Balanced: NaCl + conc. H2SO4 → NaHSO4 + HCl
marking_schemes.model_answer: The balanced equation for laboratory preparation of HCl: NaCl + conc. H2SO4 → NaHSO4 + HCl (below 200°C).
common_errors: Many incorrectly used higher temperatures
Some gave the equation for heating above 200°C (NaCl + H2SO4 → Na2SO4 + 2HCl)
Some wrote incorrect products or formulas
Some provided multiple incorrect equations
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Emphasize the products formed with different temperature conditions: below 200°C gives NaHSO4 + HCl; above 200°C gives Na2SO4 + HCl. Provide practice writing equations with conditions.

marking_schemes.scheme_text: Upward displacement of air / downward delivery / of gas.
key_points: HCl gas is denser than air — collected by upward displacement of air (downward delivery into the collecting vessel)
marking_schemes.model_answer: HCl gas is collected by the upward displacement of air (downward delivery). Since HCl is denser than air, it sinks and displaces air upward out of the collection vessel.
common_errors: Many provided incorrect answers such as upward displacement of gas or downward delivery of air
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Emphasize that HCl gas is denser than air, causing it to displace air upward during collection. Explain the process of gas collection and the reason for it.

key_points: Concentrated H2SO4 is non-volatile (very high boiling point)
Being non-volatile, it displaces the more volatile HCl gas from the sodium chloride without itself evaporating
marking_schemes.model_answer: The property of sulphuric acid that makes it a suitable reagent for this reaction is its non-volatile (least volatile) nature. Its very high boiling point means it stays in the reaction vessel and drives off the more volatile HCl gas.
common_errors: A few incorrectly described it as a dehydrating agent or a dibasic acid — these are not the relevant properties here
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Familiarize students with various properties of sulphuric acid — focus on five different properties each with an equation. The non-volatile nature is the specific property relevant to this reaction.
